summary: Defines a flag bit in the DNSKEY record to mark a key as a Secure Entry Point (SEP). It helps tell such keys apart from other keys when exchanging keys with the parent and when generating DS records. It updates RFC 2535 and RFC 3755, and was replaced by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

plainLanguage.summary: Some keys act as the front door of a signed zone. This adds a small marker so people know which key is the front-door one.

questions: what is the dnskey sep flag
how to mark secure entry point dnssec
subtitle: A flag in DNS keys to mark which ones anchor signed zones to their parents.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC requires some keys to act as entry points between a zone and its parent, but operators need a way to distinguish these from other keys in the same set.
tldr.mechanism: A single bit flag (bit 15 in the DNSKEY flags field) marks a key as a Secure Entry Point (SEP), helping operators and tools identify which keys to publish to the parent zone.
tldr.outcome: The SEP flag simplifies key management procedures and was later consolidated into updated DNSSEC standards.

facts.label: SEP bit value
facts.value: 1 to mark a Secure Entry Point key

facts.label: Used for
facts.value: Marking keys for parent zone delegation and trust anchor configuration

today: RFC 3757 defined the SEP flag concept, which was later consolidated into the updated DNSSEC specifications: RFC 4033, RFC 4034, and RFC 4035.

sections.title: The Problem: Many Keys, One Door
sections.content: DNSSEC uses keys to sign DNS data. In a deployment, a zone might hold many DNSKEY records—some for signing the zone data itself, others for operating as trusted roots. The Delegation Signer (DS) record at the parent zone points to child zone keys, but only the special ones that act as Secure Entry Points (SEP). Without a flag, there was no machine-readable way to tell which DNSKEY records should be used to generate DS records or distributed as trust anchors.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a building with many locks and keys. Some keys are just for the rooms inside, but one special key is the front-door key. You need a label so people know which is which.

sections.title: The SEP Flag
sections.content: The RFC assigns bit 15 in the DNSKEY flags field as the Secure Entry Point (SEP) bit. When set to 1, it signals that the key is intended for use as a SEP. The bit sits within the same 16-bit flags field that carries the Zone Key (ZK) bit and other DNSKEY flags. Operators can recognize a SEP key by looking at whether the flag field is even or odd in decimal.
sections.plainLanguage: It is one bit in a number. If the number is odd, the key is a front-door key.

sections.title: How Operators Use the SEP Flag
sections.content: When creating a key pair, the operator sets the SEP bit at generation time. Changing the bit later will change the key's identity in DNS, so it must remain constant once the key signs data. The RFC recommends setting the SEP bit on keys that will be published to the parent zone or configured statically in resolvers as trust anchors. When signing a zone, the signer typically uses keys with the SEP bit set to sign the DNSKEY record set itself, although the same key can also sign the rest of the zone. The SEP bit enables automated key rollover: the parent can use an existing trust relation to recognize when a new SEP-marked key appears and generate a new DS record without manual intervention.
sections.plainLanguage: When you make a new front-door key, you mark it at the start. Then the key stays marked. When you need a new one, the parent zone can see the new mark and know to use it.

sections.title: Security Notes
sections.content: The SEP flag is for administrative purposes only; it plays no role in DNSSEC verification. Verifiers should not treat a key differently based on the flag. The flag provides a hint about key intent, but trust must come from an existing chain of trust or out-of-band exchange, never from the flag itself. One risk is that automated key-rollover mechanisms using the SEP flag can be vulnerable to replay attacks if a zone sends multiple SEP keys to the parent. The RFC urges parents to implement replay defense, such as tracking which keys have been used to generate DS records in recent rollovers.
sections.plainLanguage: The mark does not make a key safe or unsafe. Real trust comes from somewhere else. But if you swap keys a lot, someone might trick you into using an old key again.
